gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, using measured inputs (Starlink Mini about 21 W average per Wirelessmoves, MacBook Air M4 about 3.3 W in Notebookcheck's 150-nit Wi-Fi test, and BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 at about 80% usable at double-digit-watt loads per techreviewer.de), one 8-hour workday uses about 195 Wh and a 1,024 Wh station lasts about 4.2 workdays, not the 1.9 days ChatGPT gave.
standout_why: I compared against starsurf.com and kilohour.com, ChatGPT's own answers, and the Starlink help pages it cited. None of them has a measured laptop figure. ChatGPT assumed 10–25 W for a MacBook Air and 450 Wh a day. Starsurf has no laptop at all and uses a flat 0.85 factor with 35 W for the Mini. Kilohour has no laptop, uses 33 W for the Mini, and applies the same 90%/95% defaults to every model. No page applies a station's own tested efficiency at a 20–30 W load, and none works out days at a measured duty cycle.
decides: The days are shorter than the rated figure suggests, because the station loses more at low loads. The light-day load is also about half what ChatGPT assumed. So a 1 kWh LiFePO4 station with two 20 V/5 A USB-C ports (BLUETTI Elite 100 V2, $499, 25 lb) covers about 4 light workdays, or about 2 at the worst case (Mini at 40 W, MacBook at max brightness). That makes the 2 kWh, 40–52 lb class ChatGPT suggested for 'multi-day' unnecessary unless the dish runs 24 h (about 1.5 days per charge). A 200 W kit panel refills a light day in about 1 h at its nameplate output.

findings.label: Starlink Mini measured average draw
findings.value: 21 W average (range 21–40 W; peaks above 40 W for the first 1–2 min after power-on)
findings.source_title: Starlink Mini – Part 2 – Power and Performance (Wirelessmoves)
findings.note: Wirelessmoves ran the Mini from an Anker power station and read the draw there. It names no meter and doesn't say which side of the station it measured.

findings.label: MacBook Air 13 M4 average draw during light work (derived)
findings.value: 3.3 W at 150 nits; 7.6 W at max brightness
findings.source_title: Notebookcheck: Apple MacBook Air 13 M4 entry review
findings.note: 53.8 Wh ÷ 16.22 h (Wi-Fi test at 150 cd/m²) = 3.3 W; 53.8 Wh ÷ 7.08 h (max brightness) = 7.6 W. Notebookcheck also measured 29.9 W average under full load, which is not a workday average.

findings.label: Energy for one 8-hour workday (derived)
findings.note: Light: 8 h × (21 W + 3.3 W) = 195 Wh. Worst case: 8 h × (40 W + 7.6 W) = 381 Wh. Dish left on 24 h: 21 W × 24 + 3.3 W × 8 = 531 Wh.

findings.label: Usable energy at low (double-digit-watt) loads
findings.note: Same review: 946 Wh drawn at a constant 500 W. Below that, self-consumption weighs more, and usable energy falls to about 80% at loads 'in the double digits'. 1,024 × 0.80 = 819 Wh.

findings.label: USB-C ports able to power the Mini (20 V/5 A)
findings.note: The Mini and the MacBook can each have a 20 V/5 A port without the AC inverter.

findings.label: Workdays per charge (derived)
findings.value: 4.2 light / 2.1 worst case / 1.5 with dish on 24 h

findings.label: Price, weight, Wh per lb, cost per workday
findings.value: $499; 25 lb; 32.8 usable Wh/lb; $119 per light workday of storage
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 Portable Power Station | 1,800W 1,024Wh (BLUETTI US store)
findings.note: storecheck shows $499, in stock. The maker page lists 1,024 Wh, 11.5 kg (25 lb), and 1,000 W solar max. 819 ÷ 25 = 32.8 Wh/lb; $499 ÷ 4.2 = $119.

findings.label: Hours of kit-panel sun to refill one workday (derived)
findings.value: about 1.0 h light / 1.9 h worst case, at the 200 W panel's nameplate
findings.note: Kit $699. 195 Wh ÷ 200 W = 0.98 h; 381 ÷ 200 = 1.9 h. Real panel output falls short of nameplate, and I found no measured derate.

findings.label: Price and rated capacity; rated-only workdays
findings.value: $499 (compare-at $1,232); 1,152 Wh; at most 5.9 light workdays at the rated figure
findings.source_title: BLUETTI AC180 Solar Portable Power Station | 1,800W 1,152Wh (BLUETTI US store)
findings.note: storecheck data. 1,152 ÷ 195 = 5.9 at rated capacity. I opened no low-load test, so the real figure will be lower, about 4.7 if the Elite 100 V2's 80% applied (not measured on the AC180).

findings.label: Kit price with its own 200 W panel
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2+200W Solar (BLUETTI US store)
findings.note: storecheck data, in stock. Same refill math as the Elite 100 V2 kit: about 1 h of nameplate sun per light workday.

findings.label: US store listing
findings.value: The Explorer 1000 v2 did not appear in a jackery.com search. HomePower 1000 v2 (1,024 Wh) lists at $549 (compare-at $1,049).
findings.note: storecheck search for 'Explorer 1000 v2' on jackery.com. The 1000 v2 may have been renamed; I didn't confirm that.

unsourced: Starlink's own published Mini average (rivals cite 25–40 W). The starlink.com help pages and the Mini product page returned no text to WebFetch, and the spec-sheet PDF couldn't be parsed, so I used Wirelessmoves' measured 21–40 W instead.

Measured usable Wh at a low (20–50 W) USB-C load for the AC180, Elite 200 V2, Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 and EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max. I found a low-load figure only for the Elite 100 V2 (techreviewer.de).
AC180 weight and USB-C port ratings from the maker page (bluettipower.com returned HTTP 429 twice).
DC/USB-only standby draw for any candidate. BLUETTI gives 4.5 W only for the Elite 30 V2, and the Cybershack 10 W figure for the Elite 100 V2 is an assumption, not a measurement.
Today's maker-store prices for the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 (anker.com storecheck returned 404) and the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max (not checked; out of call budget).
A measured real-world yield for BLUETTI's 200 W kit panel, so refill hours are given at nameplate only.
A measured light-work average for a MacBook Pro 14/16. Only the Air M4 was sourced.
